newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Exit U.S. envoy, enter Chirac in Mideast peace bid.
newsitem.headline: Exit U.S. envoy, enter Chirac in Mideast peace bid.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton's Middle East peace envoy said he was going home on Monday, having failed to break a stalemate in Israeli-PLO talks after 15 days of trying.

As Dennis Ross pulled up stakes, French President Jacques Chirac pitched his tent for three days of talks in Israel and Palestinian-ruled territories aiming to be Washington's co-sponsor of peace moves.
"I will be returning to the United States today," said Ross, sent to the region by Clinton after an outbreak of Israeli-Arab violence.

Ross said the sides were making progress on the main sticking point -- a long-promised Israeli troop pullback from Hebron, the last and most sensitive of seven West Bank cities in a 1995 accord due to be handed over to Palestinian rule.

"There were hopes that we could finalise in some areas. That didn't materialise," Ross told a news conference. A diplomatic source suggested Ross wanted to leave early to avoid devaluing his influence during slow-moving talks.
Ross said formal talks in Eilat in Israel and Taba in Egypt, along with informal discussions, had reached a level of specificity that made his involvment less important.

He said other U.S. diplomats would remain actively involved, adding he would "return when I think the time is right and appropriate." He said there were still "delicate issues" to be negotiated but declined to elaborate.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office had no immediate comment on Ross's announcement. But Palestinians insisted his departure did not signify a crisis.

"I don't think Ross's departure is an attempt to apply pressure on the negotiators from both sides and it is also not reflective of a crisis in the talks, which will continue," PLO negotiator Hassan Asfour told Reuters. Ross agreed.
Ross said the sides had agreed to resume talks on Tuesday.

An outbreak of West Bank and Gaza violence that claimed the lives of 60 Arabs and 15 Israelis in September prompted Clinton to call a White House summit attended by Netanyahu and Arafat and to send Ross to the region.
A PLO official said Washington would continue to be represented in the talks by U.S. Ambassador to Israel Martin Indyk and U.S. Consul-General in East Jerusalem Edward Abington.
Chirac arrived in Israel on Monday to a cool welcome from a right-wing government that bluntly rejects his bid for a European role as co-sponsor of Middle East peacemaking.
Asked if Europe could play a co-sponsor's role, Ross said: "I think that it is generally agreed by the parties and by others that the efforts that we are making is one that they support."

Chirac's visit was preceded by a string of diplomatic incidents that bared raw feelings on both sides about France's "Arab policy" and Israel's rejection of any further territorial concession to its Arab neighbours.
Israel's Jerusalem Post daily greeted him with an editorial calling him a "biased would-be broker" who showed "fawning support of the region's most unregenerate terrorist states".
A defiant junior French minister visited the PLO headquarters in Arab East Jerusalem, lending support to Palestinian claims to the holy city which Israel calls its eternal capital.
Chirac sent junior health minister Herve Gaymard to the PLO's Orient House headquarters after Israel refused to let Foreign Minister Herve de Charette make the trip.

"The meaning of my visit here today is...to say that as long as permanent settlement of the Palestinian question has not been achieved, the status quo applies concerning the status of Jerusalem," Gaymard said.

Israel captured Arab East Jerusalem in the 1967 Middle East war and annexed it in a move the international community refused to recognise. The PLO regards East Jerusalem as the capital of a future Palestinian state.
